[LLM] vm2 sandbox-escape PoC strings observed in inbound HTTP request body / WAF Exploitation High
Hunts the exact JavaScript token sequence from the CVE-2026-47131 PoC (Buffer.call.call/__lookupGetter__/__lookupSetter__ + WebAssembly.compileStreaming + e.constructor.constructor + mainModule.require) in web request URLs and bodies traversing the WAF / reverse proxy. Targets any service that hands user-supplied JS to a vm2 sandbox. Rationale: PoC body in the advisory cites the exact strings Buffer.call.call({}.__lookupGetter__, Buffer, "__proto__"), WebAssembly.compileStreaming(), e.constructor.constructor, and new HostFunction("return process")().mainModule.require("child_process").execSync — those tokens together don't appear in legitimate JSON payloads or REST API traffic. The narrow string set keeps FPs near zero. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v6mx-mf47-r5wg • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-47131
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb.Web
// Defender has no inbound HTTP-body table; pivot via DeviceNetworkEvents to Node processes that received the payload then look at child shells

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wmic.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("echo pwned","child_process","execSync")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let PocTokens = dynamic(["__lookupGetter__","__lookupSetter__","Buffer.call.call","compileStreaming","e.constructor.constructor","mainModule.require","child_process\").execSync"]);

  CommonSecurityLog

  | project TimeGenerated, Source="CEF", DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP=SourceIP, DestinationIP, Url=RequestURL, Method=RequestMethod, Evidence=coalesce(Message, RequestURL)
),
(
  W3CIISLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

)

[LLM] Node.exe spawning OS shell after vm2 sandbox exploitation Installation High
Hunts the post-exploit signature of CVE-2026-47131: a Node.js process spawning cmd/powershell/bash/sh with command lines containing the PoC's distinctive 'echo pwned' marker or child_process.execSync invocations. Node legitimately shells out occasionally for build tooling, so we anchor on the PoC string and the unusual integrity-level / parent-tree combination. Rationale: The PoC ends with execSync("echo pwned", { stdio: "inherit" }) — a near-unique marker — preceded by mainModule.require("child_process"). The node→shell parent-child plus those two string tokens together is article-specific and won't fire on normal Node build steps. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v6mx-mf47-r5wg

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| order by files desc

ImFileEvent

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")

            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)

| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] The Gentlemen ransomware: creation of 'gentlemen_system' SYSTEM scheduled task Installation High
Hunts for the unique scheduled task name 'gentlemen_system' that The Gentlemen ransomware (Storm-2697) registers to relaunch its encryptor under the SYSTEM account before locking local drives. Per Microsoft Threat Intelligence the malware first deletes any existing task with this name and then immediately triggers a fresh one, so both delete and create operations on this exact task name are high-fidelity signals. Rationale: 'gentlemen_system' is a unique string named explicitly by Microsoft Threat Intelligence as the SYSTEM-context task this family registers — no legitimate product uses this task name. Cross-checked against the article tables and the Microsoft persistence-screenshot image referenced as 'The Gentlemen ransomware's persistence mechanism'. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/topic/threat-intelligence/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1134.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "gentlemen_system"
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "gentlemen_system"
| where FileName in~ ("schtasks.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("schtasks.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AccountSid, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "gentlemen_system"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| union (Event
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventLog =~ "Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/Operational"
    | where EventID in (106, 140, 141, 200, 201)
    | where EventData has "gentlemen_system" or RenderedDescription has "gentlemen_system"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, RenderedDescription)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] The Gentlemen ransomware: mass file rename to .umc16h and README-GENTLEMEN.txt drop Actions on Objectives High
Hunts the in-progress encryption phase of The Gentlemen — the malware appends the unique '.umc16h' extension to every encrypted file and drops a 'README-GENTLEMEN.txt' ransom note in each directory. Either string alone is essentially zero-FP because they are operator-chosen, sample-specific markers. Rationale: Both '.umc16h' (operator-chosen build extension) and 'README-GENTLEMEN.txt' (family-specific ransom-note filename) are direct quotes from the article's IOC table and have no benign equivalent — high-confidence, low-FP encryption signal. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486/
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".umc16h" or FileName =~ "README-GENTLEMEN.txt"
| summarize EncryptedCount = count(), NotesDropped = countif(FileName =~ "README-GENTLEMEN.txt"), DistinctDirs = dcount(FolderPath), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SampleFiles = make_set(FileName, 5) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where EncryptedCount > 10 or NotesDropped > 0
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "umc16h" or TargetFileName =~ "README-GENTLEMEN.txt"
| summarize EncryptedCount = count(), NotesDropped = countif(TargetFileName =~ "README-GENTLEMEN.txt"), DistinctDirs = dcount(TargetFilePath), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| where EncryptedCount > 10 or NotesDropped > 0

[LLM] The Gentlemen ransomware encryptor execution by SHA256 + LOCKER_BACKGROUND env Installation High
Hunts process executions whose SHA256 matches the published The Gentlemen encryptor binary OR whose command line / environment block carries the internal 'LOCKER_BACKGROUND=1' flag the SYSTEM-context worker sets when running as the background encryption process. Rationale: SHA256 is the canonical encryptor hash directly from the article IOC table; 'LOCKER_BACKGROUND=1' is documented in the article as the internal SYSTEM-context background-execution flag; '9VoAvR7G' is the hardcoded build-specific operator password — all three are unique strings unlikely to appear in benign telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/topic/threat-intelligence/

   or InitiatingProcessSHA256 == "22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67"
   or ProcessCommandLine has "LOCKER_BACKGROUND=1"
   or ProcessCommandLine has "9VoAvR7G"

| order by Timestamp desc

| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] The Gentlemen persistence: UpdateSystem/UpdateUser tasks + GupdateS/GupdateU Run keys Installation High
Hunts the article's documented persistence layer for The Gentlemen ransomware: scheduled tasks named 'UpdateSystem' and 'UpdateUser' that relaunch the payload at startup as SYSTEM and as the current user respectively, paired with HKLM/HKCU Run-key values 'GupdateS' and 'GupdateU'. Looking for either artefact in isolation provides high confidence; both together is conclusive. Rationale: 'UpdateSystem', 'UpdateUser', 'GupdateS' (HKLM), and 'GupdateU' (HKCU) are all listed in the article's IOC table as Gentlemen-specific persistence artefacts — paired naming pattern (System vs User scope) is operator-chosen and not used by legitimate Google Update or any standard Windows component despite the similar-looking name. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1547/001/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Registry
let TaskHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "schtasks.exe" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Register-ScheduledTask","schtasks")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\"UpdateSystem\"","/TN UpdateSystem","/tn UpdateSystem","\"UpdateUser\"","/TN UpdateUser","/tn UpdateUser"," UpdateSystem "," UpdateUser ")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Artefact = "Task";
let RegHits = DeviceRegistryEvents

    | where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
    | where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run", @"\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run")
    | where RegistryValueName in~ ("GupdateS","GupdateU")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName=InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine=RegistryValueData, Artefact = strcat("Run:", RegistryValueName);
union TaskHits, RegHits
| order by Timestamp desc
let TaskHits = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

    | where (NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe")
    | where CommandLine has_any ("UpdateSystem","UpdateUser")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Artefact = "Task";
let RegHits = ImRegistryEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

union TaskHits, RegHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] The Gentlemen self-propagation: C:\Temp\psexec.exe + admin-share staging + multi-method remote exec Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the self-propagation worker that stages the encryptor binary into admin shares and fires 21 remote-execution attempts per target host across PsExec, WMIC, scheduled tasks, services, and PowerShell remoting. Anchored on the specific staging path C:\Temp\psexec.exe named in the article plus near-simultaneous admin-share writes from the same host within a short window — pattern that distinguishes Gentlemen's redundant-fan-out worm behaviour from one-off lateral movement. Rationale: The article explicitly names 'C:\Temp\psexec.exe' as the staging path the worker drops and references binary staging into shared folders + 21 remote-execution attempts per host across 8 methods. Combining the specific staging path with high-fan-out admin-share writes from a single source host distinguishes Gentlemen's worm behaviour from routine admin PsExec use (which is in the existing-rule exclusion list). Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0029/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1570 T1047
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
let WindowMin = 10m;
let StagingFromSource = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
    | where FolderPath startswith @"\\" and (FolderPath has @"\ADMIN$\\" or FolderPath has @"\C$\\") 
    | where FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".tmp"
    | summarize RemoteHostCount = dcount(tostring(extract(@"\\\\([^\\]+)\\", 1, FolderPath))), SampleTargets = make_set(FolderPath, 6), Count = count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, WindowMin)
    | where RemoteHostCount >= 3;
let PsExecFromTemp = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FolderPath =~ @"C:\Temp" and FileName =~ "psexec.exe"
         or ProcessCommandLine has @"C:\Temp\psexec.exe"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256;
StagingFromSource
| join kind=fullouter (PsExecFromTemp | summarize PsExecHits = count() by DeviceName) on DeviceName
| order by Timestamp desc
let WindowMin = 10m;
let Staging = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
    | where TargetFilePath startswith @"\\" and (TargetFilePath has @"\ADMIN$\\" or TargetFilePath has @"\C$\\")
    | where TargetFileExtension in~ ("exe","tmp")
    | summarize RemoteHostCount = dcount(tostring(extract(@"\\\\([^\\]+)\\", 1, TargetFilePath))), SampleTargets = make_set(TargetFilePath, 6), Count = count() by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMin)
    | where RemoteHostCount >= 3;
let PsExecHits = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where NewProcessName =~ @"C:\Temp\psexec.exe" or CommandLine has @"C:\Temp\psexec.exe"
    | summarize PsExecCount = count() by Computer, SubjectUserName;
Staging
| join kind=fullouter (PsExecHits | project DvcHostname = Computer, PsExecCount) on DvcHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*C:\\Temp\\psexec.exe OR *C:\\temp\\PsExec.exe OR *C:\\Temp\\PsExec.exe) OR @CommandLine:(*C:\\Temp\\psexec.exe* OR *C:\\Temp\\PsExec.exe*))) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(\\\\*\\ADMIN\$\\* OR \\\\*\\C\$\\*) @TargetFilename:(*.exe OR *.tmp))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (ImageFileName=/C:\\Temp\\psexec\.exe$/i OR CommandLine=/C:\\Temp\\psexec\.exe/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
| join({
  #event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/^\\\\[^\\]+\\(ADMIN\$|C\$)\\/i (TargetFileName=/\.exe$/i OR TargetFileName=/\.tmp$/i)
  | groupBy([aid], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true, as=remoteWrites))
  | remoteWrites >= 3
}, field=aid)
ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=t count values(Filesystem.dest_file_path) as paths dc(Filesystem.dest) as remoteHostCount from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path IN ("\\\\*\\ADMIN$\\*","\\\\*\\C$\\*") (Filesystem.file_name="*.exe" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.tmp") by Filesystem.src Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where remoteHostCount >= 3 | append [ | tstats summariesonly=t count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*C:\\Temp\\psexec.exe*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Filesystem.dest_file_path) as paths dc(Filesystem.dest) as remoteHostCount from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path IN ("\\\\*\\ADMIN$\\*","\\\\*\\C$\\*") (Filesystem.file_name="*.exe" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.tmp") by Filesystem.src Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where remoteHostCount >= 3 | append [ | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*C:\\Temp\\psexec.exe*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`]
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)

            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

    object payload signature.

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match · Article-specific behavioural hunt — JINX-0164 Threat Actor Using LinkedIn Social Engineering to Deploy Custom macOS
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port

| order by conn_count desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count

    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

let BadHashes = dynamic(["0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba10875f5", "a35d2b67fa478a7174e308b43ce30bf69b3bc6f44fa76197fdf95fc2fbc1cf7d", "65cba741fe30fa4799fb9002ea8de6d96042a59159dd7c3419c766af24c7a8b4", "0b1a36a31b952341a534fe24890f1ed2921ee259773cff46e4f6273b8c4d5e3a", "e8ee6f5145c9d503c5130bfc6585567f6e19d409158c3c0ca0b259f1875b1a2f", "3e3901519c2305fbe9d5483b7234c25c6d2b562512916481d96f26b849c7d4e1", "9c2ce925133a3bf5a924063bbef8df49918d5b7258695c1894cd18c75970157a", "402625ec79e3573a80b6de9b33fc1e503e3c7803603cd958ddd515fb0e4a3c91", "b6cab0b3aa8e56e2427f486c74588d598ae58bb0cbc0eda6939fe171cb4f2d89", "d4e863f9818bfb2f1dd932df6441dff204e6142c3bdb55b298cb08dc7b6a9f12", "c6ef82d2864dfd26f117a1ef5602679153423f2742970a7949cec72722f0a0b3", "2a10ffe0367bb1b26ba2c3bc600892c21074725c0b8c9dc9161e6ceb339f4d5c"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

2026-05-29 19 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Megalodon malicious GitHub Actions workflow file written to repo · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Attackers Abuse Trusted Developer Tooling to Exfiltrate Source Code and Secrets
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Nx Console v18.95.0 payload — kitty/cat.py backdoor file drop · [LLM] macOS LaunchAgent kitty-monitor persistence · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] GitHub Search API dead-drop C2 polling (firedalazer marker) · [LLM] Megalodon C2 IP egress — 216.126.225.129:8443 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] AWS IMDS access from VS Code / Node / Bun developer tooling · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
[LLM] Nx Console v18.95.0 payload — kitty/cat.py backdoor file drop Installation High
Detects creation of the Python C2 backdoor (cat.py) and its persistence artifacts at the specific kitty path used by the compromised Nx Console v18.95.0 extension (CVE-2026-48027). Article-specific paths apply to macOS, Linux and Windows variants of the dropper. Rationale: Anchored on the exact filenames and parent directories listed in the article IOC table (cat.py under kitty/, kitty-monitor.plist LaunchAgent, .gh_update_state anti-replay state file, /tmp/kitty-* staging). Cross-checked with CISA alert and the nrwl/nx-console GHSA-c9j4-9m59-847w advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/05/28/supply-chain-compromises-impact-nx-console-and-github-repositories • https://github.com/nrwl/nx-console/security/advisories/GHSA-c9j4-9m59-847w • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/nx-console-vs-code-extension-compromised • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/compromised-nx-console-18950-targeted.html
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.006 T1543.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FolderPath has @"\.local\share\kitty" and FileName =~ "cat.py")
     or (FolderPath has "/.local/share/kitty" and FileName =~ "cat.py")
     or (FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents" and FileName =~ "com.user.kitty-monitor.plist")
     or (FolderPath startswith "/tmp/kitty-")
     or (FolderPath has "/var/tmp" and FileName =~ ".gh_update_state")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (TargetFilePath has "kitty" and TargetFileName =~ "cat.py")
     or (TargetFilePath has "/LaunchAgents/" and TargetFileName =~ "com.user.kitty-monitor.plist")
     or TargetFilePath startswith "/tmp/kitty-"
     or (TargetFilePath has "/var/tmp" and TargetFileName =~ ".gh_update_state")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName,
          ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Nx Console Malicious Payload kitty/cat.py Backdoor File Drop
id: a4f6d2c8-91b3-4e7f-8c5a-1d9b7e3a6f02
description: Detects file creation of the Python C2 backdoor (cat.py) and its persistence artifacts at the kitty path used by the compromised Nx Console v18.95.0 extension (CVE-2026-48027).
references:
  - https://cybersecuritynews.com/attackers-abuse-trusted-developer-tooling/
  - https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/05/28/supply-chain-compromises-impact-nx-console-and-github-repositories
  - https://github.com/nrwl/nx-console/security/advisories/GHSA-c9j4-9m59-847w
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/29
tags:
  - attack.t1195.001
  - attack.t1059.006
  - attack.t1543.001
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection_kitty_cat:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\.local\share\kitty\cat.py'
      - '/.local/share/kitty/cat.py'
  selection_plist:
    TargetFilename|contains: '/Library/LaunchAgents/com.user.kitty-monitor.plist'
  selection_anti_replay:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '/var/tmp/.gh_update_state'
  selection_tmp:
    TargetFilename|startswith: '/tmp/kitty-'

[LLM] GitHub Search API dead-drop C2 polling (firedalazer marker) Command & Control High
Detects the Nx Console Python backdoor polling GitHub's commits-search API using the operator-specific marker token 'firedalazer' to receive signed remote commands. The marker is unique to this campaign and unlikely to appear in benign traffic. Rationale: The string 'firedalazer' is a campaign-unique search marker the backdoor embeds in the GitHub commits-search API query (api.github.com/search/commits?q=firedalazer). It has no benign meaning, so a single hit is high-fidelity. Cross-checked with StepSecurity write-up and CISA bulletin. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/05/28/supply-chain-compromises-impact-nx-console-and-github-repositories • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/nx-console-vs-code-extension-compromised • https://corgea.com/research/nx-console-vscode-extension-credential-stealer-may-2026
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1071.001 T1568
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
// Process-attributed network shape — the dead-drop poll always carries q=firedalazer
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "api.github.com"
| where RemoteUrl has "firedalazer"
   or AdditionalFields has "firedalazer"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpHostName has "api.github.com"
| where Url has "search/commits" and Url has "firedalazer"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url,
          HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpMethod, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Megalodon C2 IP egress — 216.126.225.129:8443 Command & Control High
Detects outbound TCP connections to the Megalodon credential exfiltration C2 server (216.126.225.129:8443). Every connection from a corporate device to this IP+port pair is high-fidelity given the IP has no legitimate use. Rationale: 216.126.225.129:8443 is published in CISA's advisory and the article IOC table as the Megalodon C2 for credential exfiltration. Single-IOC IP/port match — no legitimate corporate traffic should reach this destination. Cross-checked with CISA advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/05/28/supply-chain-compromises-impact-nx-console-and-github-repositories • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/nx-console-vs-code-extension-compromised • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/github-breach-nx-console-vs-code/
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "216.126.225.129"
| where RemotePort == 8443 or RemotePort == 443
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            ConnectionCount = count(),
            BytesSentTotal = sum(tolong(extract(@"BytesSent.{0,3}(\d+)", 1, AdditionalFields)))
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
               InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "216.126.225.129"
| where DstPortNumber in (8443, 443)
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            ConnectionCount = count(), TotalBytes = sum(NetworkBytes)
            by DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber,
               EventProduct
| order by FirstSeen desc

[LLM] AWS IMDS access from VS Code / Node / Bun developer tooling Actions on Objectives Medium
Detects access to the AWS instance-metadata service (169.254.169.254) or ECS task-role endpoint (169.254.170.2) initiated by developer tooling (VS Code, node, bun, python launched from a code workspace). The Nx Console payload uses this exact path to harvest AWS credentials on infected developer workstations and CI runners. Rationale: Article explicitly lists 169.254.169.254 (AWS IMDS) and 169.254.170.2 (ECS task-role) as targets of the credential-harvest module. Pairing the well-known credential-theft endpoint with developer-tooling parent processes filters out legitimate cloud-SDK use in EC2 workloads. Cross-checked with CISA advisory and StepSecurity write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/05/28/supply-chain-compromises-impact-nx-console-and-github-repositories • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/nx-console-vs-code-extension-compromised • https://corgea.com/research/nx-console-vscode-extension-credential-stealer-may-2026
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1078.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("169.254.169.254", "169.254.170.2")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("code", "node", "bun", "python", "python3", "electron")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName has_any ("code", "Code Helper", "node", "bun")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("169.254.169.254", "169.254.170.2")
| join kind=inner (
    ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("code", "node", "bun", "python", "python3", "electron")
       or ParentProcessName has_any ("code", "Code Helper", "node", "bun")
    | project DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessId, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
) on DvcHostname
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr,
          ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
(@network.destination.ip:(169.254.169.254 OR 169.254.170.2) OR @DestinationIp:(169.254.169.254 OR 169.254.170.2)) AND (@Image:(*\\Code.exe OR *\\code.exe OR *\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR *\\bun.exe OR *\\Bun.exe OR *\\python.exe OR *\\python3.exe) OR @process.executable.path:(*/Code* OR */node OR */bun OR */python OR */python3 OR */Code\ Helper*) OR @ContextImageFileName:(*\\Code.exe OR *\\node.exe OR *\\bun.exe OR *\\python.exe OR *Code\ Helper*))
(#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 OR #event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP6) RemoteAddressIP4=/^169\.254\.(169\.254|170\.2)$/
| ContextImageFileName=/(\\Code\.exe|\\node\.exe|\\bun\.exe|\\python(3)?\.exe|\/Code|\/node|\/bun|\/python(3)?|Code Helper)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=count())
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
# Detects AWS API calls authenticated with credentials freshly minted from IMDS — pivot from endpoint hit.
fields @timestamp, eventName, eventSource, userIdentity.type, userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName, sourceIPAddress, userAgent
| filter userIdentity.type = "AssumedRole"
      and userIdentity.sessionContext.attributes.mfaAuthenticated = "false"
      and (sourceIPAddress not like /^10\./ and sourceIPAddress not like /^172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[0-1])\./ and sourceIPAddress not like /^192\.168\./)
      and userAgent not like /aws-sdk-go-internal/
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 200

[LLM] macOS LaunchAgent kitty-monitor persistence Installation High
Detects creation or modification of the com.user.kitty-monitor.plist LaunchAgent at ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ — the exact persistence mechanism the Nx Console Python backdoor installs on macOS to survive reboots. Rationale: The plist filename com.user.kitty-monitor.plist combined with the ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ path is unique to this campaign per the article IOC table. No legitimate macOS application uses this naming. Verified against CISA bulletin and the nrwl/nx-console GHSA advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/05/28/supply-chain-compromises-impact-nx-console-and-github-repositories • https://github.com/nrwl/nx-console/security/advisories/GHSA-c9j4-9m59-847w • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/compromised-nx-console-18950-targeted.html

[LLM] Megalodon malicious GitHub Actions workflow file written to repo Delivery Medium
Detects checkout/clone of a Megalodon-tainted repository: a SysDiag.yml or Optimize-Build.yml file appearing under .github/workflows/. The Megalodon campaign mass-injected these specifically-named workflows into 5,561 repositories on 2026-05-18; the names are not used by any well-known CI template. Rationale: SysDiag and Optimize-Build are the article's named Megalodon workflow filenames (mass + targeted variants). The combination of .github/workflows/ path and exact filename is article-specific and would only appear on a host that cloned/pulled a tainted repo. Cross-checked with CISA advisory which urges audit of workflow files for commits after 2026-05-18. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/05/28/supply-chain-compromises-impact-nx-console-and-github-repositories • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/nx-console-vs-code-extension-compromised • https://www.ox.security/blog/teampcp-strikes-again-how-a-trojan-vs-code-extension-brought-down-github/

          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc

         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "43f2b001846c4966073ebffa5be8f15e491a1e7d32bbd805d57406ff540e0dd9") or SHA1 in~ ("1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "43f2b001846c4966073ebffa5be8f15e491a1e7d32bbd805d57406ff540e0dd9") or MD5 in~ ("1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "43f2b001846c4966073ebffa5be8f15e491a1e7d32bbd805d57406ff540e0dd9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "43f2b001846c4966073ebffa5be8f15e491a1e7d32bbd805d57406ff540e0dd9") or SHA1 in~ ("1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "43f2b001846c4966073ebffa5be8f15e491a1e7d32bbd805d57406ff540e0dd9") or MD5 in~ ("1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "43f2b001846c4966073ebffa5be8f15e491a1e7d32bbd805d57406ff540e0dd9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "43f2b001846c4966073ebffa5be8f15e491a1e7d32bbd805d57406ff540e0dd9"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
