| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:

      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

Hackers Use Fake Adobe Document Cloud Pages to Deliver ScreenConnect Malware

Cyber Security News
2026-05-29 13 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A sophisticated phishing campaign is actively targeting financial organizations by using fake Adobe Document Cloud pages to silently install ScreenConnect remote access malware on victim machines. The operation is well-structured, deceptive, and difficult to detect because it blends into everyday enterprise software activity. The campaign works by sending phishing emails that look like legitimate Adobe [&#8230;] The post Hackers Use Fake Adobe Document Cloud Pages to Deliver ScreenConnect Malware appeared first on Cyber Security News .

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1027 T1190 T1219 T1566 T1566.001

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] RatPressto phishing-kit URL paths on compromised WordPress hosts (/download.html, /complete.php, /download.php) · [LLM] Browser/email-client drop of ScreenConnect installer or victim-named VBS dropper (RatPressto silent download) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hackers Use Fake Adobe Document Cloud Pages to Deliver ScreenConnect Malware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] ScreenConnect MSI install via msiexec from user-writable temp/Downloads (RatPressto delivery) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ScreenConnect agent beaconing to RatPressto C2 (TCP/8041 to zistopstoabetterlife.com / 177.154.191.148 / 84.32.41.64) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
[LLM] RatPressto phishing-kit URL paths on compromised WordPress hosts (/download.html, /complete.php, /download.php) Delivery High
Hunts browser hits to the RatPressto stage-1/stage-2 URI paths on the specific compromised/actor-controlled WordPress domains named by Fortra FIRE. The path triplet (download.html → complete.php → download.php) plus the IOC domain set is the cleanest article-specific lure fingerprint. Rationale: Article explicitly names download.html / complete.php / download.php as the kit's three deployment files (stage-1, stage-2, hidden iframe) on the listed compromised WordPress hosts. Combining the path triplet with the IOC domain set yields a near-zero-FP fingerprint.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1189

title: RatPressto Fake Adobe Phishing Kit URL Paths
id: 7a2f3b1c-4d8e-4f60-9c1a-5e8b9a2d1f01
description: Detects browser/proxy hits to the RatPressto phishing kit stage paths (/download.html, /complete.php, /download.php) on Fortra-FIRE-named compromised WordPress hosts that deliver ScreenConnect installers.
references:
  - https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-fake-adobe-document-cloud-pages/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/29
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1566.002
logsource:
  category: proxy
detection:
  selection_path:
    cs-uri-stem|endswith:
      - '/download.html'
      - '/complete.php'
      - '/download.php'
  selection_host:
    cs-host|contains:
      - 'zistopstoabetterlife'
      - 'ampliawifi.com'
      - 'gaheempreendimentos.com'
      - 'iconclinic.ae'
      - 'kinorot.co.il'
      - 'vetcarebd.xyz'
      - 'nabellacouture.com'
      - 'birexo.icu'
      - 'abpmed.com'
  condition: selection_path and selection_host
level: high
source:(windows.sysmon OR proxy OR zscaler) (@http.url:(*/download.html OR */complete.php OR */download.php) OR @url:(*/download.html OR */complete.php OR */download.php)) AND (@http.url_details.host:(zistopstoabetterlife.com OR ampliawifi.com OR gaheempreendimentos.com OR iconclinic.ae OR kinorot.co.il OR vetcarebd.xyz OR nabellacouture.com OR birexo.icu OR abpmed.com) OR @network.destination.name:(zistopstoabetterlife.com OR ampliawifi.com OR gaheempreendimentos.com OR iconclinic.ae OR kinorot.co.il OR vetcarebd.xyz OR nabellacouture.com OR birexo.icu OR abpmed.com))
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(zistopstoabetterlife|ampliawifi|gaheempreendimentos|iconclinic|kinorot|vetcarebd|nabellacouture|birexo|abpmed)/i
| join(query={#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort=443}, field=[aid], include=[RemoteAddressIP4,ContextImageFileName])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

Catches the RatPressto execution stage: msiexec launched against a ScreenConnect installer staged in %TEMP%, %APPDATA%, or %USERPROFILE%\Downloads, including the victim-renamed variants observed (ceo.msi, microsoftceo.exe, ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi). Pivots specifically on path + filename rather than generic msiexec usage. Rationale: Article names msiexec from temp directories as the documented infection-chain pivot and lists ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi, ceo.msi, microsoftceo.exe, and CapraAssetManagementInc.vbs as the specific dropper artefacts. Tying msiexec to those exact strings keeps FPs near zero versus a generic 'msiexec from temp' hunt.
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1204.002 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ScreenConnect.ClientSetup", "ceo.msi", "microsoftceo", "CapraAssetManagement")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has ".msi" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Temp", "Downloads", "AppData\\Local", "AppData\\Roaming"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sccm.exe","ccmexec.exe","msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "msiexec.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("ScreenConnect.ClientSetup", "ceo.msi", "microsoftceo", "CapraAssetManagement")
   or (CommandLine has ".msi" and CommandLine has_any ("\\Temp\\", "\\Downloads\\", "\\AppData\\"))
| where ParentProcessName !endswith "ccmexec.exe" and ParentProcessName !endswith "TrustedInstaller.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] ScreenConnect agent beaconing to RatPressto C2 (TCP/8041 to zistopstoabetterlife.com / 177.154.191.148 / 84.32.41.64) Command & Control High
High-confidence C2 detection on the self-hosted ScreenConnect relay called out in the article: TCP/8041 to *.zistopstoabetterlife.com, the São Paulo IP 177.154.191.148, or 84.32.41.64. Catches both the install-time relay arg and the steady-state agent heartbeat. Rationale: Article explicitly states the C2 is cloud.zistopstoabetterlife.com on TCP/8041 with São Paulo hosting at 177.154.191.148 and an associated 84.32.41.64. Three IOCs + non-standard port make this a high-confidence alert with negligible FP risk.

| where (RemotePort == 8041 and RemoteIPType == "Public")
   or RemoteUrl has "zistopstoabetterlife.com"
   or RemoteIP in ("177.154.191.148", "84.32.41.64")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (DstPortNumber == 8041 and DstIpAddr !startswith "10." and DstIpAddr !startswith "192.168." and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.")
   or DstHostname has "zistopstoabetterlife.com"
   or DstIpAddr in ("177.154.191.148", "84.32.41.64")

[LLM] Browser/email-client drop of ScreenConnect installer or victim-named VBS dropper (RatPressto silent download) Delivery Medium
Detects the hidden-iframe download stage: browsers or Outlook writing a ScreenConnect MSI, microsoftceo.exe, ceo.msi, or a company-name-prefixed .vbs into Downloads/Temp/AppData. Catches the kit's victim-customised filenames (e.g. CapraAssetManagementInc.vbs). Rationale: Article calls out that the iframe silently drops ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi and that file names are customised to match the victim's business context (microsoftceo.exe, ceo.msi, CapraAssetManagementInc.vbs are explicit examples). Watching for browser/email writes of these exact names — or a company-name-style VBS — directly fingerprints the kit.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"

| rename All_Email.recipient as user

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

Legitimate-Looking Codex Remote UI Steals OpenAI Codex Authentication Tokens

Cyber Security News
2026-05-29 9 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A polished, fully functional npm package has been caught secretly stealing OpenAI Codex authentication tokens from developers who trusted it. The package, named codexui-android, presented itself as a remote web UI for OpenAI Codex with no obvious signs of being malicious. It built a genuine user base, amassed 27,000 weekly downloads, and maintained an active [&#8230;] The post Legitimate-Looking Codex Remote UI Steals OpenAI Codex Authentication Tokens appeared first on Cyber Security News .

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Legitimate-Looking Codex Remote UI Steals OpenAI Codex Authentication Tokens
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] codexui-android npm package install or chunk-PUR7OUAG.js write on developer host · [LLM] Android emulator / WSL extracts Linux rootfs and runs node.exe pulling unpinned npm
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound traffic to BrutalStrike Codex stealer C2 (anyclaw.store /startlog) · [LLM] HTTP POST to /startlog with XOR+base64 stealer beacon shape · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

[LLM] HTTP POST to /startlog with XOR+base64 stealer beacon shape Command & Control High
Detects the specific HTTP POST shape used by the codexui-android stealer: a POST to a URL ending in /startlog on the anyclaw.store infrastructure (or any host) carrying a base64-encoded XOR("anyclaw2026") body. Catches actor infrastructure pivots where they reuse the same path but rotate the domain. Rationale: Article + IOC table specify POST /startlog as the exfil endpoint. Pairing the path with codexui-android-typical parents (node, npm, electron, java for the Android app) lowers FP risk vs path-only matching. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/legitimate-looking-codex-remote-ui/

[LLM] Codex auth.json read followed by outbound HTTP within 60s (token theft pattern) Actions on Objectives Medium
Temporal correlation: a node.exe or related JS runtime reads the user's Codex auth.json credential file, then within 60 seconds initiates an outbound HTTPS POST. Matches the codexui-android stealer's exact behaviour of loading at module init, reading auth.json, XOR+base64 encoding, and posting to the C2 — without needing the C2 domain itself, so survives infra rotation. Rationale: Article states the malicious code 'fired the moment the tool launched' and 'targeted the auth.json file stored at the user's Codex home directory' then sent contents to attacker server. The auth.json + same-process outbound POST within 60s captures the behaviour even if the C2 domain changes. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/legitimate-looking-codex-remote-ui/

[LLM] Android emulator / WSL extracts Linux rootfs and runs node.exe pulling unpinned npm Installation Medium
Detects the codexui-android Android app's distinctive on-host execution chain: an Android emulator or WSL process extracts rootfs.tar.zst.bin into private storage, then spawns node.exe which runs `npm install codexui-android` (or similar) with no version pin, pulling whatever the current malicious build is at runtime. This is the second-stage delivery vector described for the 'OpenClaw Codex Claude AI Agent' app. Rationale: Article details the Android app extracts a Linux env, runs Node.js, and installs the malicious npm package 'without pinning a version'. rootfs.tar.zst.bin is the named userland archive; gptos.intelligence.assistant and codex.app are the named Play Store package IDs; app.anyclaw.* is the shared Kotlin namespace — all from the IOC table. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/legitimate-looking-codex-remote-ui/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1195.002 T1027.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
union isfuzzy=true
( DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName =~ "rootfs.tar.zst.bin" or FileName endswith ".tar.zst.bin"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, EventKind="rootfs-drop"),
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName =~ "node.exe" or FileName =~ "npm.exe" or FileName =~ "npx.exe"
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "codexui-android"
     or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "app.anyclaw"
     or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "gptos.intelligence.assistant"
     or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "codex.app"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, EventKind="node-pulls-codexui")
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
( DeviceFileEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where FileName =~ "rootfs.tar.zst.bin"
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=DeviceName, User=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Process=InitiatingProcessFileName, Cmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, EventKind="rootfs-drop"),
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

  | where ProcessCommandLine has "codexui-android" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("gptos.intelligence.assistant","codex.app","app.anyclaw")
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=DeviceName, User=AccountName, Process=InitiatingProcessFileName, Cmd=ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, EventKind="node-pulls-codexui"),

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

2026-05-29 13 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have discovered a malicious NuGet package that masquerades as a C# software development kit for Sicoob, one of Brazil's largest cooperative financial systems, to siphon client IDs and PFX certificates. According to Socket, versions 2.0.0 through 2.0.4 of "Sicoob.Sdk" contain functionality to exfiltrate sensitive information, including PFX certificates that are used to

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Sicoob.Sdk malicious NuGet package present on developer host (v2.0.0–2.0.4) · [LLM] Installation of vpmdhaj-published npm credential-stealer packages (14 known names) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] npm install lifecycle script reads AWS/Vault/CI credentials within minutes of package install · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound HTTPS or DNS to Sicoob/npm-cluster exfil domains (aab.sportsontheweb.net, oob.moika.tech) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] PFX certificate read by .NET process followed by HTTPS egress to fake-Sentry domain · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
[LLM] Sicoob.Sdk malicious NuGet package present on developer host (v2.0.0–2.0.4) Delivery High
Hunts for installation/restore of the trojanised Sicoob.Sdk NuGet package on developer or build hosts. The package is published under the actor profile 'sicoob' and any version in the 2.0.0–2.0.4 range is malicious — its SicoobClient class reads PFX certs from disk and exfiltrates them to a hardcoded fake-Sentry endpoint. Rationale: Hits the article's most specific IOC — package name 'Sicoob.Sdk' restricted to the exact malicious version range 2.0.0–2.0.4 published by Socket. No other version of this package exists in production NuGet today, so a file-shape match is enough to alert without behavioural correlation.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where (FolderPath has @"\.nuget\packages\sicoob.sdk\" or FolderPath has @"\packages\sicoob.sdk\" or FolderPath has @"/.nuget/packages/sicoob.sdk/")
| extend pkgVersion = extract(@"(?i)sicoob\.sdk[\\/](\d+\.\d+\.\d+)", 1, FolderPath)
| where pkgVersion in ("2.0.0","2.0.1","2.0.2","2.0.3","2.0.4")
| where FileName endswith ".dll" or FileName endswith ".nupkg" or FileName endswith ".nuspec"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, pkgVersion, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\.nuget\packages\sicoob.sdk\" or TargetFilePath has @"\packages\sicoob.sdk\" or TargetFilePath has @"/.nuget/packages/sicoob.sdk/"
| extend pkgVersion = extract(@"(?i)sicoob\.sdk[\\/](\d+\.\d+\.\d+)", 1, TargetFilePath)
| where pkgVersion in ("2.0.0","2.0.1","2.0.2","2.0.3","2.0.4")
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("dll","nupkg","nuspec")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, pkgVersion, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] PFX certificate read by .NET process followed by HTTPS egress to fake-Sentry domain Actions on Objectives High
Behavioural detection for the Sicoob.Sdk exfil chain: SicoobClient opens a .pfx file, base64-encodes it, and POSTs the bytes plus the client ID and PFX password to aab.sportsontheweb.net (a Sentry-impersonating domain). Correlates a PFX file event with an outbound network event by the same .NET process within 5 minutes. Rationale: Combines two article-specific signals: PFX file access by a .NET runtime (Sicoob SDK consumers are dotnet/csc/w3wp), and outbound to the named C2 domain aab.sportsontheweb.net, plus the sibling C2 oob.moika.tech for the parallel npm cluster. Same-process+5-minute correlation makes this very low-noise.
ATT&CKT1552.004 T1041 T1102
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
let lookback = 30d;
let maxDelay = 5m;

| where FileName endswith ".pfx" or FileName endswith ".p12"

| project PfxTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, PfxPath=FolderPath, PfxFile=FileName;
let Egress = DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("sportsontheweb.net","moika.tech") or RemoteIP in ("")
| project NetTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessId, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort;
PfxReads

| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', NetTime, PfxTime)
| project PfxTime, NetTime, DelaySec, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, PfxPath, PfxFile, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by PfxTime desc

[LLM] npm install lifecycle script reads AWS/Vault/CI credentials within minutes of package install Installation High
Hunts the 'vpmdhaj' preinstall-hook chain plus the broader npm credential-harvester pattern. Looks for a node/npm/yarn/pnpm process touching ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.vault-token, ~/.npmrc, .env, or shell-history files within 10 minutes of an npm install kicking off — the exact behaviour Microsoft Defender Research called out for the 14 vpmdhaj packages. Rationale: Targets the exact behaviour Defender Research described for vpmdhaj's preinstall hooks (AWS keys, Vault tokens, npm tokens, CI secrets harvested from host environment), and also catches forge-jsxy and the 164-package oob.moika.tech cluster which share the same pattern. The 10-minute install-to-cred-read window cuts most legitimate dev-tool access to those files.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1059.007 T1546.016
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
let lookback = 14d;
let maxDelay = 10m;
let Installs = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.cmd","npm.exe","yarn.cmd","yarn.exe","pnpm.cmd","pnpm.exe","node.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.cmd","npm.exe","yarn.cmd","yarn.exe","pnpm.cmd","pnpm.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (" install","preinstall","postinstall"," i "," ci "," add ") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (" install","preinstall","postinstall")
| project InstallTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InstallCmd=ProcessCommandLine;
let CredHits = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where (FolderPath has @"\.aws\" or FolderPath has @"/.aws/"
      or FileName in~ (".vault-token",".npmrc",".env",".bash_history",".zsh_history")
      or FolderPath has @"\.vault" or FolderPath has @"/.vault"
      or FolderPath has @"\.docker\config" or FolderPath has @"/.docker/config"
      or FolderPath has @"\.kube\config" or FolderPath has @"/.kube/config")
| project CredTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, CredPath=FolderPath, CredFile=FileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
Installs
| join kind=inner CredHits on DeviceId
| where CredTime between (InstallTime .. InstallTime + maxDelay)
| summarize CredFilesTouched=make_set(strcat(CredPath, CredFile), 25), FirstCred=min(CredTime), LastCred=max(CredTime), Cmd=any(InstallCmd) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InstallTime
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', FirstCred, InstallTime)
| order by InstallTime desc
let lookback = 14d;
let maxDelay = 10m;
let Installs = ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("npm.cmd","npm.exe","yarn.cmd","yarn.exe","pnpm.cmd","pnpm.exe","node.exe") or ParentProcessName has_any ("npm.cmd","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (" install","preinstall","postinstall"," ci "," add ") or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any (" install","preinstall","postinstall")
| project InstallTime=TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, InstallCmd=ActingProcessCommandLine;
let CredHits = ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\.aws\" or TargetFilePath has @"/.aws/"
     or TargetFileName in~ (".vault-token",".npmrc",".env",".bash_history",".zsh_history")
     or TargetFilePath has @".vault"
     or TargetFilePath has ".docker/config" or TargetFilePath has ".kube/config"
| project CredTime=TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, CredPath=TargetFilePath;
Installs
| join kind=inner CredHits on DvcHostname
| where CredTime between (InstallTime .. InstallTime + maxDelay)
| summarize CredFilesTouched=make_set(CredPath, 25), FirstCred=min(CredTime), Cmd=any(InstallCmd) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, InstallTime
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', FirstCred, InstallTime)
| order by InstallTime desc

[LLM] Outbound HTTPS or DNS to Sicoob/npm-cluster exfil domains (aab.sportsontheweb.net, oob.moika.tech) Command & Control High
Pure IOC pivot on the two confirmed exfil domains from both campaigns — aab.sportsontheweb.net is the Sicoob.Sdk fake-Sentry endpoint, oob.moika.tech is the 164-npm-package /report beacon. Any developer, build, or CI host resolving or connecting to either domain is treated as compromised until proven otherwise. Rationale: Both domains are flagged in the article as hardcoded exfil endpoints (aab.sportsontheweb.net for Sicoob.Sdk's fake-Sentry POSTs, oob.moika.tech/report for the 164-npm-package env-var beacon). Neither is a legitimate corporate destination; any hit is high-fidelity. Wildcards on parent domains catch subdomain rotation by the actor.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)

| project Timestamp, Source="NetworkConnect", DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort),
(DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("sportsontheweb.net","moika.tech")
| project Timestamp, Source="DnsQuery", DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP=tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).IpAddress), RemotePort=int(0))
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true

| project TimeGenerated, Source="NetworkSession", DvcHostname, SrcUsername, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url),

| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Installation of vpmdhaj-published npm credential-stealer packages (14 known names) Delivery High
File-event hunt for any of the 14 npm packages published by 'vpmdhaj' (a39155771@gmail.com) on 2026-05-28 — both the scoped @vpmdhaj/* set and the typosquatting unscoped names targeting OpenSearch/ElasticSearch/DevOps users. Presence in any host's node_modules is sufficient to alert. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the 14 named packages from the article (both the @vpmdhaj/* scope and the 10 typosquatting unscoped names). Filters on package.json/index.js/preinstall.js/postinstall.js keep the alert to one event per install rather than firing for every file extracted from the tarball.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"

          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("638788afc4f1b5860a328312caf5895abd5f5632d28a4f2a85b09076e270d15d", "77d92efe7af3547f71fd41d4a884872d66b1be9499eaa637e91eac866911694d", "bfa149694ec6411c23936311a999163ade54d6f38e2f4b0e3cfb8cb67bd7cfaa") or SHA1 in~ ("638788afc4f1b5860a328312caf5895abd5f5632d28a4f2a85b09076e270d15d", "77d92efe7af3547f71fd41d4a884872d66b1be9499eaa637e91eac866911694d", "bfa149694ec6411c23936311a999163ade54d6f38e2f4b0e3cfb8cb67bd7cfaa") or MD5 in~ ("638788afc4f1b5860a328312caf5895abd5f5632d28a4f2a85b09076e270d15d", "77d92efe7af3547f71fd41d4a884872d66b1be9499eaa637e91eac866911694d", "bfa149694ec6411c23936311a999163ade54d6f38e2f4b0e3cfb8cb67bd7cfaa")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("638788afc4f1b5860a328312caf5895abd5f5632d28a4f2a85b09076e270d15d", "77d92efe7af3547f71fd41d4a884872d66b1be9499eaa637e91eac866911694d", "bfa149694ec6411c23936311a999163ade54d6f38e2f4b0e3cfb8cb67bd7cfaa") or SHA1 in~ ("638788afc4f1b5860a328312caf5895abd5f5632d28a4f2a85b09076e270d15d", "77d92efe7af3547f71fd41d4a884872d66b1be9499eaa637e91eac866911694d", "bfa149694ec6411c23936311a999163ade54d6f38e2f4b0e3cfb8cb67bd7cfaa") or MD5 in~ ("638788afc4f1b5860a328312caf5895abd5f5632d28a4f2a85b09076e270d15d", "77d92efe7af3547f71fd41d4a884872d66b1be9499eaa637e91eac866911694d", "bfa149694ec6411c23936311a999163ade54d6f38e2f4b0e3cfb8cb67bd7cfaa")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["638788afc4f1b5860a328312caf5895abd5f5632d28a4f2a85b09076e270d15d", "77d92efe7af3547f71fd41d4a884872d66b1be9499eaa637e91eac866911694d", "bfa149694ec6411c23936311a999163ade54d6f38e2f4b0e3cfb8cb67bd7cfaa"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Charter Communications data breach affects 4.9 million accounts

BleepingComputer
2026-05-29 7 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The ShinyHunters extortion gang stole personal information from 4.9 million accounts after hacking the U.S. telecom giant Charter Communications in early April, according to data breach notification service Have I Been Pwned. [...]

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Vishing-induced Entra ID sign-in from new location/IP after employee call · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] OAuth consent granted to look-alike Salesforce/Data-Loader app from compromised employee
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ShinyHunters leak-site Charter URI checked from corporate browsing
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Salesforce Bulk/REST API mass-export volume burst from newly-consented app
[LLM] Vishing-induced Entra ID sign-in from new location/IP after employee call Delivery Medium
Hunts for an Entra ID interactive sign-in following the ShinyHunters vishing pattern that compromised the Charter employee: a successful auth from an IP/ASN/country never seen for that user, often using legacy MFA flows the actor walked the victim through on the phone. Distinct from generic impossible-travel by anchoring to AuthenticationDetails / AuthenticationRequirement and same-day first-seen IP. Rationale: Article states the breach began with vishing of an employee whose Microsoft Entra account was then compromised on April 1. Detection targets that exact pivot — new-IP + new-country sign-in succeeding via interactive MFA methods that match how vishers coach victims through approving push prompts. Cross-checked with prior ShinyHunters Salesforce write-ups (Mandiant UNC6395 reporting, Google Threat Intelligence) which document help-desk vishing + push-bombing as the consistent initial access vector. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/004/
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1078.004

[LLM] OAuth consent granted to look-alike Salesforce/Data-Loader app from compromised employee Installation High
ShinyHunters' Salesforce campaign hinges on tricking the vished employee into granting OAuth consent to a connected app masquerading as 'Salesforce Data Loader' or 'My Ticket Portal'. This hunts AAD consent-grant events for app display names matching the ShinyHunters lure set, especially when granted by a non-admin and consenting to broad API/refresh-token scopes. Rationale: ShinyHunters' Salesforce-centric campaign (2024-2025) is documented by Google Mandiant (UNC6240/UNC6395) and Salesforce themselves as using lookalike OAuth apps named 'Salesforce Inc. Data Loader' or 'My Ticket Portal' to grant the actor API access without needing the victim's password again. The Charter article confirms the same actor + Salesforce data theft pattern, so this is the highest-fidelity pivot specific to this campaign — far more specific than generic 'illicit consent grant' rules. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion • https://www.salesforce.com/blog/protect-against-social-engineering/
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sourcesChange.Account_Management
let LureApps = dynamic(["Salesforce Inc. Data Loader","Data Loader","My Ticket Portal","Salesforce Data Loader","Salesforce CLI"]);
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add delegated permission grant.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.")
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).ModifiedProperties[0].NewValue)
| extend TargetApp = tostring(ObjectName)
| where TargetApp has_any (LureApps) or AppName has_any (LureApps)
   or TargetApp matches regex @"(?i)(data\s?loader|salesforce.*data|my\s?ticket\s?portal)"
| extend Consenter = AccountDisplayName, ConsenterUpn = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).UserId)
| project Timestamp, Consenter, ConsenterUpn, TargetApp, AppName, IPAddress, UserAgent, CountryCode, IsAdminOperation, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
let LureApps = dynamic(["Salesforce Inc. Data Loader","Data Loader","My Ticket Portal","Salesforce Data Loader","Salesforce CLI"]);
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OperationName in ("Consent to application","Add delegated permission grant","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant","Add app role assignment grant to user")
| extend TargetApp = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName)
| extend ConsenterUpn = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| extend ConsenterIp = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| extend ModProps = TargetResources[0].modifiedProperties
| where TargetApp has_any (LureApps)
   or tostring(ModProps) has_any (LureApps)
   or TargetApp matches regex "(?i)(data ?loader|salesforce.*data|my ?ticket ?portal)"
| project TimeGenerated, ConsenterUpn, ConsenterIp, TargetApp, OperationName, ModProps, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Salesforce Bulk/REST API mass-export volume burst from newly-consented app Actions on Objectives Medium
Detects the data-exfiltration phase of the Charter/ShinyHunters Salesforce theft: a connected app or session generating an abnormal volume of REST/Bulk API queries against Account/Contact objects within a short window. Anchors on Salesforce Event Monitoring logs ingested into CloudAppEvents / Sentinel custom tables. The 42M-record claim implies sustained Bulk API jobs the EventLogFile.API record makes visible. Rationale: Article quantifies the theft as 42M records and explicitly names Charter's Salesforce instance as the source. A bulk-export of that scale is impossible to do quietly via the UI — it must use Bulk API / REST API and shows up in Salesforce EventLogFile EVENT_TYPE=BulkApi. Cross-referenced with Salesforce's own published guidance after the 2025 ShinyHunters wave which recommends Event Monitoring queries on EVENT_TYPE=BulkApi joined to non-baselined SOURCE_IP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.salesforce.com/blog/protect-against-social-engineering/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion
ATT&CKT1530 T1567
Data sourcesWeb.Web
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| where ActionType in ("BulkApiRequest","RestApiRequest","ApiCall","ApiTotalUsage","BulkApi2")
| extend Records = tolong(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).RowsProcessed)
| extend Object = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).EntityName)
| extend ClientName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).ClientName)
| where Object has_any ("Account","Contact","Lead","Case","User")
| summarize TotalRecords = sum(Records), Calls = count(), Objects = make_set(Object), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ClientName, IPAddress, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where TotalRecords > 50000 or Calls > 1000
| order by TotalRecords desc
let SuspectApps = dynamic(["Salesforce Inc. Data Loader","Data Loader","My Ticket Portal","Salesforce Data Loader"]);
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResourceDisplayName has "Salesforce" or AppDisplayName has_any (SuspectApps)
| where ResultType == 0
| summarize SignInCount = count(), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName), IPs = make_set(IPAddress), Countries = make_set(tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion))
    by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where SignInCount > 50 or array_length(IPs) > 5
| order by SignInCount desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.resourceDisplayName:*Salesforce* @properties.status.errorCode:0
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(my\.salesforce\.com|salesforce\.com|force\.com)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=[count(), min(_time), max(_time)])
| count > 500
APPLICATION
`salesforce_eventlogfile` EVENT_TYPE IN ("API","BulkApi","BulkApi2","RestApi") | stats sum(ROWS_PROCESSED) as records dc(ENTITY_NAME) as objects values(ENTITY_NAME) as objs by USER_ID CLIENT_NAME SOURCE_IP _time span=1h | where records > 50000 OR (objects>=2 AND records>10000) | where match(objs,"(?i)(Account|Contact|Lead|Case|User)")
[LLM] ShinyHunters leak-site Charter URI checked from corporate browsing Command & Control Low
Hunts for any corporate device contacting the ShinyHunters dark-web leak site or its clearnet mirrors after the Charter listing went up — useful both to detect employees rubbernecking (insider risk / OpSec) and to catch an attacker pivoting from the same infrastructure into the network. Targets the published leak-site hostnames and Tor gateway patterns associated with the group. Rationale: Article explicitly notes ShinyHunters published the data on their dark-web leak site after Charter refused payment. Post-disclosure hunting for any corporate endpoint touching that leak site is a low-volume, high-context signal — most production environments will have zero hits, so any match warrants triage (either insider OpSec issue, or an attacker reachback from your own network). Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/charter-communications-data-breach-affects-49-million-accounts/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.003

   or RemoteUrl has_any ("onion.ws","onion.ly","tor2web.io","darkfailllnkf4vf","shinyhunters")

  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects HTTP/DNS access from corporate endpoints to the ShinyHunters extortion leak site or common clearnet Tor gateways (onion.ws / tor2web). Investigative signal post-Charter disclosure.
references:

  - attack.t1090.003
  - attack.command_and_control

  category: dns
detection:
  selection:
    query|re|i: '(shinyhunters|\.onion(\.ws|\.ly|\.cab|\.to|\.pet)?|tor2web)'
  condition: selection
level: medium
(source:zeek OR source:windows.sysmon OR source:cloudflare) (@dns.question.name:*shinyhunters* OR @dns.question.name:*onion.ws OR @dns.question.name:*tor2web* OR @http.url:*shinyhunters* OR @http.url:*onion.ws*)

NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web where Web.url IN ("*shinyhunters*","*.onion*","*tor2web*","*onion.ws*","*onion.ly*") OR Web.dest IN ("*shinyhunters*") by Web.src Web.user Web.url Web.http_user_agent _time | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.url IN ("*shinyhunters*","*.onion*","*tor2web*","*onion.ws*","*onion.ly*") OR Web.dest IN ("*shinyhunters*") by Web.src Web.user Web.url Web.http_user_agent _time | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

[LLM] Web service in container spawning interactive shell (Redis/nginx RCE) Exploitation High
Hunts CVE-2025-49844 (Redis Lua RCE) and CVE-2026-24061 (nginx) post-exploitation pattern: redis-server, nginx, node or java spawning sh/bash/busybox inside a containerised host — the unambiguous fingerprint of RCE landing inside a vulnerable image. Rationale: Article names CVE-2025-49844 (Redis Lua RCE) and CVE-2026-24061 (nginx) as the in-container exploits driving Kinsing/perfctl/Dero/Mirai/Gafgyt staging. Cross-checked against MITRE T1190 page and abuse.ch ThreatFox notes on Kinsing post-exploit shell drop patterns. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/ • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/browse/malware/win.kinsing/
ATT&CKT1190 T1203 T1059.004

| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl ","wget ","/tmp/","/dev/shm/","chmod +x","base64 -d","bash -i","|sh","|bash")

| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl ","wget ","/tmp/","/dev/shm/","chmod +x","base64 -d","bash -i","|sh","|bash")

| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Container privilege escalation via Looney Tunables, PwnKit, sudo chroot Exploitation High
Detects CVE-2023-4911 (GLIBC_TUNABLES env-var corruption), CVE-2021-4034 (pkexec PwnKit) and CVE-2025-32463 (sudo --chroot/-R) — the exact local-root chain named in the article for Kinsing and perfctl campaigns. Rationale: Article explicitly names CVE-2023-4911 (Looney Tunables, Kinsing), CVE-2021-4034 (PwnKit, perfctl) and CVE-2025-32463 (sudo). Detection anchors on the unique exploit signatures — GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc. prefix is the Looney Tunables hallmark, sudo --chroot/-R is CVE-2025-32463-specific. Cross-checked against Qualys advisory for Looney Tunables and the sudo CVE-2025-32463 advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2023/10/03/cve-2023-4911-looney-tunables-local-privilege-escalation-in-the-glibcs-ld-so • https://www.stratascale.com/vulnerability-alert-CVE-2025-32463-sudo-chroot • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1180/
ATT&CKT1068 T1548.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.")
    or (FileName =~ "pkexec" and InitiatingProcessAccountName != "root")
    or (FileName =~ "sudo" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--chroot "," -R /","--chroot="," -R="))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (ActingProcessCommandLine has "GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.")
    or (ActingProcessName endswith "/pkexec" and ActorUsername != "root")
    or (ActingProcessName endswith "/sudo" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--chroot "," -R /","--chroot="," -R="))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

references:
